newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan money to flow overseas despite dollar risk.
newsitem.headline: Japan money to flow overseas despite dollar risk.

text.p: With the lure of higher yields, Japanese institutions are expected to keep pouring money into the United States despite the risk of a falling dollar, senior currency traders and strategists say.
"Life insurers appear ready to pour another three trillion yen ($23.8 billion) into foreign bonds," said Taisuke Tanaka, market strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston.
"These plans are unlikely to be changed unless Tokyo drastically alters its macroeconomic policies and narrows the interest rate gap (with the United States)," he said.
The analysts believe that Washington -- despite public comments to the contrary -- could try to push the dollar lower in order to narrow the growing trade deficit with Japan.

"Stepped up warnings from the U.S. Treasury against a surge in Japan's trade surplus are a prelude to a strategy of pushing the dollar down to help boost the much-wounded competitiveness of U.S. exporters," said a strategist at a local investment advisory firm.
Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said here on Friday that Japan should not let its current account surplus rise sharply again.
He rejected suggestions that a stronger yen was the best way to head off a rising surplus.

Strategists, however, said that true U.S. foreign exchange policies are better reflected in the recent statements of leading U.S. economists whom they feel may be privy to the U.S. Treasury's true intentions.
"Our Treasury, at least implicitly, is now calling for (a stronger yen)," said Fred Bergsten, a former U.S. official who now heads the Institute for International Economics.
Currency traders said that Washington may wait a while before taking any action on exchange rates.

"Washington appears to be giving Japan some breathing space to achieve domestic-led growth without using exports to fuel growth," said Takeshi Hanai, executive manager of Industrial Bank of Japan Ltd's International Treasury Department.
He said that if Japan fails to achieve those objectives, the United States will signal an end to its strong-dollar policy.
Such a scenario is hardly fertile ground for increased U.S. investment, but with record low yields at home and rising rates in America, the capital outflow is expected to grow.
The yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury bond is a hefty 4.77 percentage points above the benchmark 10-year Japanese government bond.
Life insurers bought 3.43 trillion yen ($27.2 billion) in foreign bonds and stocks in 1996.
Insurers said that U.S. investment would pay off even if the dollar falls from its current level of 126 yen to 115 yen.
And they said that the U.S. market is again attractive even though Japanese investors encountered huge foreign exchange losses on foreign bond investment in the late 1980s.

"Most of the insurers that lost trillions of yen on foreign bond investments in the late 1980s finished writing off those losses in the past two years, reviving their capacity for risk-taking (in foreign bonds)," said Yoshiichi Taguchi, strategist at Tokio Marine MC Asset Management Co Ltd.

Furthermore, institutional investors have shed many of their cross-shareholdings in other Japanese companies, as planned financial reforms under Japan's "Big Bang" will render them less useful in cementing corporate ties.
Proceeds from these sales of shares have left financial firms flush with cash, much of which has been earmarked for foreign bond purchases, the analysts say.
